title: A comb with a few hairs
told: a traditional story of Guru Gobind Singh and Pir Budhu Shah

hook.say: before the story, a question. do you carry anything that reminds you of someone?
options: then you already know what today is about. listen.
then let me show you five. listen.

steps.line: In the hills lived a Muslim Sufi saint, Pir Budhu Shah, a close friend of Guru Gobind Singh. When the Guru’s people were attacked, he came to stand with them.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: Afterward, the Pir found the Guru combing his long, uncut hair with a small wooden comb, as Sikhs do each morning.

steps.q: Ask for any gift, the Guru says. The Pir asks for the comb, hairs and all. How do you think the Guru answers?
o: Says hair is too sacred to give
Gives it, and adds more gifts
Offers him a new comb instead
steps.why: He gave it gladly, and more besides. Tradition says Budhu Shah had lost two of his own sons fighting beside the Guru.

steps.line: Ask for anything, the Guru said. The Pir pointed to the comb, with a few hairs still caught in it. That one, please.
The Guru gave him the comb with the hair, and with it, tradition says, a small sword and a turban. His family kept them as treasures for generations.

steps.q: A Muslim saint standing with a Sikh Guru was dangerous in those years. What does tradition say it finally cost him?
steps.why: Sikh tradition says a Mughal official later had him killed for helping the Guru. Sikhs still honor him as a friend who paid in full.

steps.line: Initiated Sikhs carry five such things, the five Ks: kesh, uncut hair. Kanga, a comb. Kara, a steel bracelet. Kachera, cotton undershorts. Kirpan, a small sword.
steps.label: today

steps.line: None is a decoration. The kirpan stands for protecting people who can’t protect themselves. The comb, for keeping hair, and life, clean and in order.
steps.label: today

steps.q: The kara is a plain steel circle. Why a circle, many Sikhs say?
o: No beginning, no end, like God
It shows a person is married
steps.why: A circle has no start and no finish. Steel, not gold, so it’s the same on every wrist, rich or poor.

steps.q: Of the five Ks, why cotton undershorts?
o: Self-control, and being ready to move
A sign of a farming family
Respect for the cotton of Punjab
steps.why: Kachera stand for self-restraint, and they let a person ride, run or help at once, unlike a long wrapped cloth.

say: here’s what i love. the pir asked for the most ordinary thing in the tent. and that’s the point of the five ks: hair, a comb, a bracelet, plain cotton. none of it is jewelry.
sikhs keep them on the body, at work, at the gym, all day, so the reminder is never locked away in a temple. many sikhs who aren’t initiated still wear the kara.

steps.q: The Pir’s comb and a Sikh’s kanga are both plain wood. What makes them precious?
o: Being blessed by a Guru’s hand
What they make you remember each day
steps.why: Ordinary things, kept close, remind you every morning who you mean to be. That’s the five Ks, and the Pir’s comb.

today.say: today, choose one thing you already wear, a ring, a watch, a hair tie, and give it a job: when you touch it, remember who you mean to be. sikhs do this with the kara.
options: good. let your hand remember for you.
then your own wrist will do. touch it, and remember.

card.from: a traditional story of Pir Budhu Shah
sources: Sikh tradition of Pir Budhu Shah of Sadhaura, who supported Guru Gobind Singh at the battle of Bhangani (1688), and the Guru’s gift of his comb with hair, a kirpan and a turban
Sikh teaching of the five Ks (panj kakar) of the Khalsa
